---
title: "Bundle a Plugin"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Test the Skill. **Objective:** package Skills (and their evals) as a plugin, validate it, and know why installing one is a trust decision.
**Time:** about 20 minutes. <span class="ao-badge">Verified: ran `claude plugin validate .` and `--strict` on `exercises/forge/fasta-tools` (Claude Code 2.1.325). Other claims: last verified (docs, not run) on 2026-11-13, sources in `research/forge.md`.</span>
:::

A single Skill in your folder helps you. A **plugin** is a folder that bundles Skills, and optionally agents, hooks and MCP servers (add-on connections that give the agent extra tools), so a whole group can install the same set and get updates.

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

The smallest plugin is a manifest (the file that describes the plugin: its name, version and author) and one Skill. Only `name` is required in `plugin.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "fasta-tools",
  "description": "Small checks for FASTA files, as a teaching example.",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "author": { "name": "Agent Odyssey contributors" }
}
```

Layout rules that trip people up:

- Only `plugin.json` goes inside `.claude-plugin/`. Skills, agents and hooks go at the plugin root (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `agents/`, `hooks/hooks.json`). Components placed inside `.claude-plugin/` do not load.
- The plugin `name` becomes a namespace (a prefix that keeps names from clashing), so the Skill is invoked as `/fasta-tools:check-fasta`.
- Put your evals in `evals/<case>/` so they travel with the plugin.

Try it without installing anything:

```bash
claude --plugin-dir ./fasta-tools      # load for this session only
claude plugin validate ./fasta-tools   # checks files are well formed
claude plugin validate ./fasta-tools --strict   # also fails on warnings
```

After editing, run `/reload-plugins` in the session. `validate` exited 0 on the example here, with only an icon warning that matters for marketplace submission. It checks syntax and schema, not behaviour: that is what the evals in the previous quest are for.

To share, a **marketplace** (a plugin catalogue) is a repository with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` listing plugins and where to fetch them. It is a catalogue, not a hosted store. People add it once and install by name.

## OpenCode + Ollama

OpenCode has its own plugins: code (`.ts` or `.js`) that adds tools and hooks, loaded from `.opencode/plugins/` or `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`, or listed in its config as npm packages, git repositories or local directories. Last verified (docs): the config key spelling and whether OpenCode reads a Claude `plugin.json` are *unconfirmed*; check the current OpenCode docs before relying on either.

What does work across both, per the docs read: a plain `SKILL.md` under `.claude/skills/` is found by OpenCode too. If your group uses both tools, shipping the Skill that way is the portable route.

:::

## Installing one is a trust decision

::: {.callout-warning}
Per the Claude Code docs, a plugin you install can run arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges. Hooks, monitors, local MCP and language servers, and anything in `bin/` run **outside** the sandbox and the permission rules. Skills and agents only enter the context as instructions, but instructions can steer the agent too.
:::

Before installing or updating a plugin:

1. Check where it comes from. A marketplace name says who publishes it, not what the plugin does.
2. Read `hooks/hooks.json`, `.mcp.json`, and anything in `bin/`. These are where code lives.
3. In a session, `/plugin` shows what will be installed. `claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name>` lists a component inventory without a session.
4. Remember that auto-update can change files you reviewed. Pin a `version` for plugins you publish.

## When a team shares Skills

**Idea from the GitHub Blog article** "Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills" by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog), in our own words. It is advice for teams, not part of the plugin format.

- **Keep project names and conventions in one file.** The reference genome build, the sample-ID pattern and the results folder names belong in a single **project-facts file** (a plain file that lists them, not the plugin's `plugin.json`) which every Skill reads, not in each `SKILL.md`. Then another lab can reuse your Skills with its own file and no rewriting, and a rename touches one place.
- **Keep discovered details apart from team standards.** A pattern the agent finds in your code is an observation, not a rule. Store it separately, and have a person confirm it before it becomes a standard.
- **If you generate copies, check for drift.** Say you keep one source `SKILL.md` and generate copies for other tools. Run a check in CI (automated checks that run on every change) that fails when a copy no longer matches its source.
- **Blocking a merge depends on repository rules and required checks, not on the Skill alone.** Whether a bad change is stopped depends on those rules, not on instructions in a Skill. A review step written in a Skill is advice unless a required check backs it.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Plugins overview](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says what a plugin holds, its install scopes and the cost of an enabled plugin.
- [Plugin manifest reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/manifest-reference): Anthropic, docs. Why read: every plugin.json field and what claude plugin validate checks.
- [Hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks): Anthropic, docs. Why read: hooks are the plugin part that runs code, so read this before trusting one.
- [Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/build-once-run-on-any-agent-a-practical-guide-to-agent-skills/): Andrea Griffiths, GitHub Blog, article. Why read: a vendor article whose advice on one file of project facts, keeping observed patterns apart from team standards, and checking generated copies for drift is paraphrased in "When a team shares Skills"; secondary to the docs.
:::
